fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is actually a question I think about a lot, partly because "mid-training" is a term that's only really entered the vocabulary in the last couple of years, and I don't think the community has fully converged on what it means yet.

Let me start with the two ends, because those are clearer. Pre-training is the stage where you take a randomly initialized model and expose it to an enormous, mostly unfiltered corpus with a simple objective, usually next-token prediction. The goal there is breadth. You're trying to get the model to absorb as much of the structure of language and the world as possible, and you don't really care about any particular downstream behavior. It's compute-dominant: this is where the vast majority of the FLOPs go, and the data is chosen more by quantity and diversity than by careful curation.

Post-training is the other end. By that point the model already has its capabilities, and what you're doing is shaping how those capabilities are expressed. Instruction tuning, RLHF, preference optimization, safety alignment, all of that. The datasets are small, often tens or hundreds of thousands of examples rather than trillions of tokens, and they're very intentionally constructed. The objective is often not next-token prediction anymore, or at least not purely.

So where does mid-training sit? The way I think about it is that it's the stage where the data is still large-scale, still trained with the pre-training objective for the most part, but it's chosen with intent. You're no longer just scooping up the internet. You're deliberately upweighting things like math, code, long-context documents, high-quality textbooks, maybe synthetic data, and you're doing it at a scale that's big enough to actually change the model's capabilities rather than just its behavior. People sometimes call this "annealing" or "the decay phase," because it often coincides with the learning rate coming down, and in that window the model is unusually sensitive to what you show it. A relatively small amount of good data at the end can move benchmarks a lot more than the same data mixed in uniformly from the beginning.

I'd say the honest distinction isn't really about the algorithm, since you can run mid-training with exactly the same loss as pre-training. It's about three things: what fraction of the compute budget it takes, how curated the data is, and what you're trying to change. Pre-training changes what the model knows, post-training changes how it acts, and mid-training is where you try to inject new capabilities into a model that already has a foundation but hasn't been locked into a particular persona yet.

And I'll admit the boundaries are fuzzy. A lot of what gets called mid-training today would have just been called "the last ten percent of pre-training" a few years ago. The reason it's gotten its own name, I think, is that labs discovered it's a surprisingly high-leverage knob. If you have a fixed pre-trained checkpoint, which more and more people do because training from scratch is so expensive, then mid-training is really the only place left where you can still make large, capability-level interventions. That's a big part of why I find it interesting from a research standpoint: it's the stage with the highest ratio of unexplored questions to compute required.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, because I think the terms are used a bit loosely, and different labs draw the lines in slightly different places. Let me give you how I think about it.

Pre-training is the stage most people are familiar with. You take a huge amount of mostly unfiltered or lightly filtered data, like web text, books, and code, often trillions of tokens, and you train with a simple objective, usually next-token prediction. The goal is very broad. You want the model to absorb as much knowledge about the world and about language as possible, and to learn good general representations. You're not really targeting any specific behavior. You're just trying to build a strong foundation.

Post-training is at the other end. It's much smaller in compute and data, and it's about shaping behavior. That's supervised fine-tuning on instruction data, preference optimization like RLHF or DPO, and more recently a lot of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for math and code. My mental model is that post-training mostly doesn't teach the model new knowledge. It teaches the model how to use what it already has: how to follow instructions, how to format an answer, how to reason step by step, how to be safe and helpful. It elicits capabilities more than it creates them.

Mid-training is the interesting in-between stage, and I think it emerged somewhat organically. People realized there's a gap between "trained on the whole internet" and "ready to be fine-tuned into an assistant or a reasoner." So mid-training usually still looks like pre-training mechanically. It's often still next-token prediction at fairly large scale, maybe tens or hundreds of billions of tokens. But the data distribution is much more curated and targeted. You upweight high-quality data, math, code, reasoning-heavy text, sometimes synthetic data or chain-of-thought-style data. You might extend the context length or add new domains or languages. Often it coincides with the learning-rate annealing phase at the end of pre-training, which is partly why the boundary is so blurry.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: pre-training determines what the model knows, post-training determines how it behaves, and mid-training is where you shift the model's distribution so that it's well prepared for whatever you want post-training to do. And I think that last part matters more than people initially appreciated. There's growing evidence that RL in post-training works much better when the base model already shows some of the right behaviors, for example some tendency to verify or backtrack in reasoning. Mid-training is often where those seeds get planted. So it's not just a bookkeeping category. It actually changes what's achievable downstream.

That said, I wouldn't treat these as fundamentally different things. They're really points on a continuum, defined mostly by the data distribution, the scale, and the objective. As the field matures, I suspect the lines will keep moving, and what we call mid-training today might just be considered part of a well-designed pre-training curriculum in a few years.

fable-5.text:
Thanks, Ravid — great to be here. So this is actually a question where I think the field doesn't have a fully settled answer, and the boundaries are blurrier than people sometimes make them sound.

The traditional view is pretty simple: pre-training is where you take a huge amount of raw data — mostly web text — and train the model with next-token prediction to acquire general knowledge and capabilities. Post-training is where you take that base model and align it to actually be useful: instruction following, chat formatting, safety, reasoning behaviors — through supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, and these days RL with verifiable rewards.

Mid-training is the newer concept, and it sits in between, but I'd say it's defined less by a specific technique and more by its purpose and data. It's still largely next-token prediction, like pre-training, but instead of generic web data you use smaller amounts of higher-quality, more targeted data — things like math, code, long-context documents, or synthetic data designed to teach specific skills. It usually happens in the later stages of pre-training, often coinciding with learning rate annealing, where the model is especially sensitive to data quality and can absorb these targeted capabilities efficiently.

One way I like to think about it: pre-training builds the foundation of knowledge, mid-training shapes and strengthens particular capabilities on top of that foundation, and post-training elicits and aligns those capabilities into the behavior you actually want. There's an argument that post-training mostly surfaces what's already in the model rather than teaching fundamentally new things — so if you want the model to be genuinely good at, say, math reasoning, you need that competence built in during pre-training or mid-training.

But honestly, the lines keep shifting. Some labs fold what I'd call mid-training into "stage two of pre-training," others treat long-context extension or synthetic reasoning data as post-training. And with RL becoming such a big compute investment, even the pre-training versus post-training distinction is getting fuzzy. So I treat these terms as describing a spectrum — from broad, data-hungry knowledge acquisition to narrow, targeted behavior shaping — rather than three cleanly separated stages.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, I think the honest answer is that the boundaries are fuzzy, and part of why we have three names is sociological — it reflects how teams get organized more than some deep principle. But there is a real distinction underneath.

The way I think about it: pre-training is where almost all the knowledge and most of the raw capability comes in. It's web-scale, it's mostly next-token prediction, and you're buying breadth. You're not being very precious about any individual example because there are trillions of them.

Post-training is the opposite regime. Small data, very high value per example, and you're mostly not teaching the model new things — you're shaping behavior. Which format to answer in, when to refuse, how to be helpful. The superficial alignment hypothesis is probably too strong, but directionally it captures something: a lot of post-training is eliciting what's already latent rather than installing something new.

Mid-training is the thing in the middle that people kept doing without naming it. You've finished your big general run, and now you want to deliberately shift the data mixture — more code, more math, more long-context, more curated reasoning traces. Same objective as pre-training usually, still next-token prediction, still fairly large volumes, but the data is chosen rather than scraped. The annealing phase at the end of a run is the canonical example.

If I had to give one clean framing, it's about installation versus elicitation. Pre-training and mid-training install capabilities; post-training elicits and shapes them. Mid-training is where you install things you *know* you want and couldn't guarantee the web would give you in sufficient density.

The practical reason it exists as a separate stage is economic. Pre-training runs are enormously expensive and you don't want to redo one because you decided you needed better math. So mid-training is the place where you can still meaningfully change what the model knows, without paying the full cost again. That's the real constraint driving the taxonomy.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the boundaries are fuzzy, and the terms are partly a matter of convention. But roughly, I think of them in terms of what data you use, what objective you optimize, and what you want the model to get out of that stage.

Pre-training is the big one. You take a huge, diverse corpus, mostly web-scale data plus code, books, and so on, and train with next-token prediction. It takes the vast majority of the compute, and the goal is to build up general knowledge and capabilities. The model learns language, facts, and a lot of reasoning patterns, but it isn't yet shaped into something that behaves like an assistant.

Post-training is everything after that where you're shaping behavior. That includes supervised fine-tuning on instruction data, preference-based methods like RLHF, and more recently reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for math, code, and reasoning. The data is much smaller and more targeted, and the objective is often different from plain next-token prediction. You're teaching the model how to use what it already knows: follow instructions, format answers, reason step by step, and be safe and helpful.

Mid-training sits in between, and it's the least well defined. In practice it often still uses the next-token prediction objective, like pre-training, but on a different, more curated data distribution. That could be higher-quality data, or data concentrated on specific skills like math, code, or long context, usually at the end of the pre-training run, often alongside learning rate decay. You're not changing the objective so much as changing what the model sees. The idea is to strengthen certain capabilities and prepare the model for post-training, especially RL, because RL works much better if the base model already has the right foundation.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: pre-training builds broad capability, mid-training steers and sharpens it with better or more targeted data, and post-training turns it into the behavior you want. Where you draw the line between the first two, or the last two, depends on who you ask. A lot of what people call mid-training today would have just been called the last phase of pre-training a couple of years ago.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think about it in terms of what each stage is doing to the model. Pre-training is where most of the broad knowledge and general capability come from. You train on a huge, diverse corpus with a simple objective, and the model absorbs a lot of structure about language and the world. Post-training is more about shaping behavior: following instructions, the format of responses, preferences, and safety. Mid-training sits in between. You're still mostly doing next-token prediction, but you change the data mixture toward higher-quality or more targeted data, sometimes with longer context, so the model gets pushed toward particular capabilities before the behavior-shaping starts.

The lines are blurry, though. The distinction is partly about the objective and partly about the data and the goal. If you're still doing the same kind of self-supervised training with a curated mixture, is that a separate stage or just a different schedule? People use these terms inconsistently, so I don't think there's a settled answer yet. The question I find most useful is whether you're trying to add capability and knowledge or change how the model presents itself. Mid-training is more the former, which is why it's become a useful place to ask where capabilities actually come from.

I'd also push back a little on the idea that post-training is just alignment. Some reasoning ability seems to get sharpened or elicited there, and it's hard to say cleanly what was learned in that stage versus what was already latent from pre-training. We don't understand that boundary very well yet.

astra-6.text:
I think these are useful names, but the boundaries are not very sharp. The way I would distinguish them is by what you’re trying to achieve at each stage.

In pre-training, you’re building the foundation. You train on a very large amount of data, usually with a fairly general objective like predicting the next token, and the model acquires broad knowledge and capabilities.

Post-training is where you turn that foundation into something that behaves the way you want. For a conversational assistant, that could mean following instructions, giving useful answers, or improving through feedback and reinforcement learning.

Mid-training is a somewhat less well-defined term. Usually it means additional training between those stages, where you change the data distribution to develop particular capabilities. You might emphasize math or code, introduce more domain-specific data, or train the model to handle longer contexts. The objective can still look very similar to pre-training, but the data and the purpose are more targeted.

So I wouldn’t think of these as three fundamentally different algorithms. Often the distinction is more about the data, the objective, and where the training fits in the overall process. And some of the same capabilities can be improved at more than one stage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as stages along a continuum, rather than three completely different things. Pre-training is where you build the general foundation. You train on a broad distribution of data, usually with a next-token prediction objective, and the model develops a lot of its knowledge and capabilities.

Mid-training is a less precisely defined term. Usually it means you’re continuing to train that foundation, but changing the data distribution to emphasize particular capabilities. That might mean more code, more mathematical content, or longer sequences. You’re still doing something quite similar to pre-training, but you’re becoming more deliberate about what you want the model to learn.

Post-training is where you more directly shape how the model behaves when someone interacts with it—following instructions, producing useful answers, and improving through feedback or rewards.

But those boundaries are blurry. Post-training can teach new capabilities, and pre-training data can already contain instruction-following examples. So I would distinguish them more by their purpose and the training signal than by simply where they appear in the pipeline.

I think of them as three different phases with different objectives. Pre-training is where you give the model a huge, broad corpus and teach it the basic statistical structure of language, code, and the world. It’s mostly about scale and coverage.

Post-training is the familiar alignment stage: instruction tuning, preference optimization, reinforcement learning—making the model more helpful, safe, and better at following what users actually want.

Mid-training sits between them. The model already has the basic capabilities from pre-training, but before you optimize it for chat behavior, you can use carefully selected, higher-quality data to strengthen particular abilities: reasoning, coding, long-context understanding, multilingual skills, or domain knowledge. It’s a way of reshaping the model’s capabilities more deliberately than generic pre-training, while keeping it distinct from the behavioral alignment goals of post-training.

Post-training is more about how those capabilities are expressed: instruction tuning, preference optimization, and safety training teach the model to follow requests, be useful, and behave according to human or product preferences. The boundaries aren’t perfectly sharp, but that capability-versus-behavior distinction is a useful way to think about it.
